Strangled
strang'gld
a. and v. (killed without the shedding of blood; one of the four abstentions the Jerusalem council laid on Gentile believers)
From Latin strangulare, to choke, through Old French estrangler. The Greek at Acts 15:20 is pniktos, choked or throttled — the adjective for an animal killed without draining its blood.

Biblical Definition

Three of the four occurrences belong to one decision. The council at Jerusalem, having settled that Gentiles are not to be circumcised or put under the law of Moses for salvation, wrote to them: “that they abstain from pollutions of idols, and from fornication, and from things strangled, and from blood” (Acts 15:20), and in the letter itself, “That ye abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication: from which if ye keep yourselves, ye shall do well” (Acts 15:29). James repeats the four to Paul years later (Acts 21:25). A strangled animal is one killed without the blood being drained, and the prohibition therefore belongs with the one beside it. Its ground is older than Moses: “But flesh with the life thereof, which is the blood thereof, shall ye not eat” (Genesis 9:4), given to Noah for all mankind, and explained in Leviticus — “the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls” (Leviticus 17:11). Nahum uses the word of a lion: he “strangled for his lionesses” (Nahum 2:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines strangle as to choke, to suffocate, to destroy life by stopping respiration — and notes the scriptural prohibition of things strangled.

expand to see more

STRANGLED, pp. Choked; suffocated.

STRANGLE, v.t. To choke; to suffocate; to destroy life by stopping respiration.

Our Saviour was strangled by the cross.

2. To suppress; to hinder from birth or appearance.

STRANGLING, ppr. Choking; suffocating; suppressing.

Key Scripture

Acts 15:20 — "But that we write unto them, that they abstain from pollutions of idols, and from fornication, and from things strangled, and from blood."

Acts 15:29 — "That ye abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication: from which if ye keep yourselves, ye shall do well. Fare ye well."

Genesis 9:4 — "But flesh with the life thereof, which is the blood thereof, shall ye not eat."

Leviticus 17:11 — "For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul."

Modern Corruption

The four abstentions are read either as a permanent food law or as pure social diplomacy, and the doctrine underneath them — the sanctity of blood — is missed either way.

expand to see more

Two readings of Acts 15 have long competed. One takes the four abstentions as binding dietary law still, which sits awkwardly with Paul's own teaching in Romans 14 and 1 Corinthians 8 that no meat is unclean of itself. The other treats them as purely diplomatic — concessions to Jewish sensibilities in mixed congregations, with no doctrinal content. Neither is adequate. Fornication in the same list is not a matter of table fellowship, and the blood prohibition is not Mosaic in origin: it was given to Noah, for all humanity, before Abraham and before Sinai. The council is naming things that predate the law it has just declared not binding for salvation.

The doctrinal weight is in Leviticus 17:11. Blood is prohibited because the life of the flesh is in the blood and because God assigned it to the altar for atonement. To treat blood as ordinary food is to treat as common the very thing God set apart to signify a life given for a life — which is why Hebrews can say that without shedding of blood is no remission. Whatever a congregation concludes about eating black pudding, the reason for the reverence should not be lost, and the New Testament nowhere weakens it: we are redeemed not with corruptible things, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek pniktos, strangled or choked — Acts 15:20, 29, 21:25; haima, blood; Hebrew nephesh, life or soul — Leviticus 17:11; dam, blood — Genesis 9:4.

expand to see more

Greek pniktos — choked, strangled; only in the three Acts references to the council's decree.

Greek haima — blood; the companion prohibition, and the word of the atonement in Hebrews.

Hebrew dam — blood; Genesis 9:4, in the covenant with Noah.

Hebrew nephesh — life, soul; Leviticus 17:11, “the life of the flesh is in the blood.”

Hebrew kaphar — to cover, to make atonement; the purpose God assigned to blood.

Usage

"“From things strangled, and from blood” — the two prohibitions belong together."

"“Flesh with the life thereof… shall ye not eat” — given to Noah, before Sinai."

"“It is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul” — the reason underneath."
